Reference: Jia, Ma and Xie (2026)

Model Setting

The paper asks how flood risk, as opposed to realized flood events, shapes where firms locate and how much people work, and what this implies for aggregate output. Using county-level and zip-code-level US data for 1998-2018, the authors document two facts: (i) a rise in flood risk has a large, negative long-run effect on firm entry, employment and output; (ii) realized floods reduce output in the year they occur but have little effect on firm entry or employment. Flood risk is measured from digitized FEMA maps: the historic Q3 Flood Insurance Rate Maps for 1998 and the National Flood Hazard Layer for 2018. The measure is the share of a county's (or zip code's) land inside Special Flood Hazard Zones, which are areas with at least a 1 percent annual chance of inundation. On average this share rose by 6 percentage points between 1998 and 2018, and by 19 percentage points at the ninetieth percentile of county changes. Flood events come from the Dartmouth Flood Observatory (DFO). Firm entry, exit and employment come from the Census Business Dynamics Statistics, prime-age population from the Census, county real GDP from the BEA, and zip-code outcomes from the Zip Codes Business Patterns. The facts motivate a quantitative spatial model with Krugman (1980) free entry and McFadden (1978) location choice. Firms and workers make long-run decisions before floods are realized and anticipate flood risk; realized floods lower productivity and amenities and destroy some firms. In the calibrated model, flood risk lowered US aggregate output by 0.53 percent in 2018. Direct damages account for 23 percent of this loss and long-run adjustment by firms and workers for 77 percent.

Reduced-Form Evidence: Flood Risk

The baseline specification, estimated on the two years t∈{1998,2018}t\in\{1998,2018\}t∈{1998,2018}, is:

log⁡Yi,t=α+β1 FloodRiski,t+σi+γs,t+ζXi,t+β2 ActualFloodi,t+ϵi,t(9.7.1.1)\log Y_{i,t}=\alpha+\beta_1\,\text{FloodRisk}_{i,t}+\sigma_i+\gamma_{s,t}+\zeta X_{i,t}+\beta_2\,\text{ActualFlood}_{i,t}+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{9.7.1.1}logYi,t​=α+β1​FloodRiski,t​+σi​+γs,t​+ζXi,t​+β2​ActualFloodi,t​+ϵi,t​(9.7.1.1)

Here Yi,tY_{i,t}Yi,t​ is firm entrants (or exits, employment, population, real GDP) in locality iii (county or zip code), and FloodRiski,t\text{FloodRisk}_{i,t}FloodRiski,t​ is the share of land in FEMA special flood zones. σi\sigma_iσi​ are locality fixed effects and γs,t\gamma_{s,t}γs,t​ state-by-year fixed effects. Xi,tX_{i,t}Xi,t​ contains controls in the spirit of Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013): female labor share, manufacturing employment share, population density and China import penetration. ActualFloodi,t\text{ActualFlood}_{i,t}ActualFloodi,t​ is the cumulative share of flooded area. Standard errors are clustered by locality. At the county level (5,072 observations, with controls) the coefficients are −0.169-0.169−0.169 (0.080) for entry, −0.111-0.111−0.111 (0.074) for exit, −0.199-0.199−0.199 (0.054) for employment, −0.130-0.130−0.130 (0.042) for population and −0.278-0.278−0.278 (0.070) for output. A one-standard-deviation (10-percentage-point) rise in flood risk therefore lowers entry by 1.7 percent, employment by 2.0 percent, population by 1.3 percent and real GDP by 2.8 percent. A county at the ninetieth percentile of risk increases loses 3.3 percent of entry. Exits fall because there are fewer firms and less business dynamism. Employment responds more than population, so the remaining residents also cut labor supply; bilateral commuting data show this is not driven by commuting. At the zip-code level (41,032 observations) the coefficients are −0.203-0.203−0.203 for establishments, −0.250-0.250−0.250 for employment and −0.225-0.225−0.225 for payroll. A placebo on 1990-1998 outcomes gives small and insignificant estimates. Two checks address endogenous FEMA map revisions and measurement error. A cross-fit partialing-out LASSO-IV uses ERA5-Land geo-climatic variables for 1998 (air and soil temperature, precipitation, evaporation, vegetation), the average risk change in the rest of the state, and their interactions as candidate instruments. It gives −0.214-0.214−0.214 (entry), −0.124-0.124−0.124 (exit), −0.253-0.253−0.253 (employment), −0.143-0.143−0.143 (population) and −0.338-0.338−0.338 (output), against OLS change-on-change estimates of −0.169-0.169−0.169, −0.111-0.111−0.111, −0.199-0.199−0.199, −0.130-0.130−0.130 and −0.278-0.278−0.278. A property-weighted measure built from First Street Foundation's 2018 model-based maps and 1998 Q3 maps overlaid with GHSL population rasters gives larger estimates: −0.556-0.556−0.556, −0.522-0.522−0.522, −0.568-0.568−0.568, −0.363-0.363−0.363 and −0.570-0.570−0.570.

Reduced-Form Evidence: Flood Events

On a balanced county panel for 2001-2018 (49,376 observations), the authors estimate:

log⁡Yi,t=α+β1 Floodi,t+σi+γs,t+ζXi,t+ϵi,t(9.7.1.2)\log Y_{i,t}=\alpha+\beta_1\,\text{Flood}_{i,t}+\sigma_i+\gamma_{s,t}+\zeta X_{i,t}+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{9.7.1.2}logYi,t​=α+β1​Floodi,t​+σi​+γs,t​+ζXi,t​+ϵi,t​(9.7.1.2)

where Floodi,t\text{Flood}_{i,t}Floodi,t​ is the share of county area flooded in year ttt. Realized floods have negligible effects on entry (0.001), exit (0.003), employment (−0.001-0.001−0.001) and population (0.001). They do lower real GDP: the coefficient is −0.005-0.005−0.005 (0.002), and a one-standard-deviation (0.4) rise in flooded share cuts same-year GDP by 0.2 percent. Lagged floods have negligible effects. The model therefore treats realized floods mainly as productivity shocks, while expected risk drives long-run decisions.

Model: States of Nature and Timing

The economy has MMM regions indexed by mmm (counties), and total population is normalized to Lˉ=1\bar{L}=1Lˉ=1. A set of states of nature S={s1,s2,…}S=\{s_1,s_2,\ldots\}S={s1​,s2​,…} is given. Each state sss has probability Pr⁡(s)\Pr(s)Pr(s) and a vector of flood indicators {ξ1(s),…,ξM(s)}\{\xi_1(s),\ldots,\xi_M(s)\}{ξ1​(s),…,ξM​(s)}, with ξm(s)∈{0,1}\xi_m(s)\in\{0,1\}ξm​(s)∈{0,1}. The flood risk of region mmm is its flood probability:

rm=∑sPr⁡(s) ξm(s)(9.7.1.3)r_m=\sum_s\Pr(s)\,\xi_m(s) \tag{9.7.1.3}rm​=s∑​Pr(s)ξm​(s)(9.7.1.3)

The timing has two stages. Before shocks are realized, individuals choose a location and how much labor to supply, and firms decide whether to enter. After shocks are realized, floods lower productivity and amenities, a fraction of firms exits, and the remaining firms produce while individuals work and consume. Insurance is not modeled. Firms are risk neutral, so actuarially fair insurance would only reflect expected damages and would not change entry decisions. The authors also note that NFIP coverage excludes business interruption.

Higher risk damages productivity, firm count and amenities. The variety channel matters for welfare but is not captured in GDP data. Relocation losses in origin regions are largely offset by gains in destination regions, so migration matters much less in the aggregate than locally.

Calibration: External Parameters

Each region is a county, and the calibration targets 2018; the counties used account for 96 percent of US GDP. The elasticity is σ=5\sigma=5σ=5, the mean trade estimate in Head and Mayer (2014), which implies a markup of 0.25. The baseline exit rate is κˉ=0.08\bar{\kappa}=0.08κˉ=0.08, from County Business Patterns. Flood risk rmr_mrm​ must be in the same units as realized flooded shares, because land in a flood zone can flood more often than 1 percent of the time. The authors therefore regress county-year flooded shares in 2015-2019 on 2018 flood-zone shares and use the fitted intercept and slope to convert zone shares into flood probabilities. The mean of rmr_mrm​ is 0.18 (s.d. 0.10). The same conversion gives rm,1998r_{m,1998}rm,1998​ from 1998 maps. The damage parameters come from the event regressions, summing current-year and one-year-lag effects: δ=0.006\delta=0.006δ=0.006 (GDP) and δk=0.008\delta_k=0.008δk​=0.008 (exits). There are no county amenity data, so the amenity loss uses Barrage (2020), where output damages are about three times direct utility damages in DICE; hence η=0.002\eta=0.002η=0.002, about one third of δ\deltaδ. The value of η\etaη matters little for national output, because it mainly moves people between regions.

Calibration: Internal Parameters and Identification

The model is calibrated in levels rather than with exact hat algebra, for consistency with the trade extension, where bilateral flows are unobserved. Exact hat algebra in the baseline gives very similar results. National GDP, population and firm count are normalized to one. In an inner loop, given {ϕM,ϕL}\{\phi_M,\phi_L\}{ϕM​,ϕL​}, four region-specific vectors are fit exactly to county data: Aˉm\bar{A}_mAˉm​ (mean 2.40, s.d. 2.53) to real GDP, Bˉm\bar{B}_mBˉm​ (0.41, 0.65) to population, ψm\psi_mψm​ (0.35, 0.34) to the employment-to-population ratio, and fmf_mfm​ (0.09, 0.03) to firm count. The model-data correlation is close to one for all four sets of targeted moments. In an outer loop, the elasticities are chosen by indirect inference (Gourieroux and Monfort 1996). The model is re-solved with flood probabilities {rm,1998}\{r_{m,1998}\}{rm,1998​}, and the Table 1 panel regressions of log employment and log population on flood risk are re-run on simulated 1998 and 2018 data. This yields ϕL=1.55\phi_L=1.55ϕL​=1.55 and ϕM=0.84\phi_M=0.84ϕM​=0.84. Identification is transparent from Proposition 2. The employment response pins down the total labor elasticity, and the gap between employment and population responses separates labor supply per person (ϕL\phi_LϕL​) from migration (ϕM\phi_MϕM​). The implied elasticity of population with respect to real wages, ϕM(1+ϕL)≈2.1\phi_M(1+\phi_L)\approx 2.1ϕM​(1+ϕL​)≈2.1, lies inside the 1.1-2.5 range surveyed by Fajgelbaum, Morales, Suarez Serrato and Zidar (2018). Calibrated amenities are high in Arizona and California and low in the central US. Productivity is high in New York, California and Washington and low in Mississippi and Alabama, and the two are barely correlated, in line with Allen and Arkolakis (2014).

Model Fit

The targeted coefficients are employment −0.199-0.199−0.199 (model −0.199-0.199−0.199) and population −0.130-0.130−0.130 (model −0.117-0.117−0.117). The nontargeted ones are output −0.278-0.278−0.278 (model −0.205-0.205−0.205, closer to the zip-code estimates), entry −0.169-0.169−0.169 (model −0.201-0.201−0.201, since entry mirrors employment) and exit −0.111-0.111−0.111 (model −0.194-0.194−0.194). The model reproduces the negative exit response. Higher risk raises the closure probability of a given firm, but it lowers entry by more, so total exits fall.

Counterfactual 1: Aggregate Effects of Flood Risk in 2018

The baseline equilibrium is compared with one in which rm=0r_m=0rm​=0 for all mmm. Flood risk lowers aggregate output by 0.53 percent, employment by 0.33 percent, firm entry by 0.30 percent, firm exits by 0.15 percent and welfare by 0.52 percent. The decomposition lets channels adjust one at a time. First, direct damages alone are computed holding labor supply and population fixed. Then population shares, labor supply and the number of varieties move in turn to their no-risk levels. Direct damages account for 0.12 percent of output, close to the FEMA estimate of about 17 billion dollars per year in 2010-2018, roughly 0.1 percent of GDP. That is only 23 percent of the total. Labor relocation accounts for 0.02 percent, because inflows and outflows offset. Lower labor supply accounts for 0.31 percent (58 percent of the loss), and fewer varieties for 0.08 percent (15 percent). Ignoring the long-run adjustment of firms and workers therefore greatly understates the loss.

Counterfactual 2: Distributional Effects

The national loss hides large heterogeneity. The top 5 percent and top 1 percent of counties ranked by output loss lose 9.1 percent and 15.9 percent of output; examples include coastal places such as Cape May, New Jersey. Direct damages concentrate in southern and eastern, especially coastal, counties. In the top 1 percent of counties population falls by 7.1 percent, labor supply per person by 5.4 percent and the number of firms by 12.5 percent. Mildly exposed counties, such as some in the Midwest, are winners: they gain migrants, firm entry and, because more varieties raise utility, labor supply per worker.

Extensions

  • Entry costs in goods: entry costs become fmWm(s)1−αPm(s)αf_m W_m(s)^{1-\alpha}P_m(s)^{\alpha}fm​Wm​(s)1−αPm​(s)α, where α\alphaα is the share paid in final goods. Final-good prices respond more to flood risk than wages do, so entry falls more as α\alphaα rises. With α=1\alpha=1α=1 the output loss is 0.57 percent (entry −0.56-0.56−0.56 percent, welfare −0.57-0.57−0.57 percent), against 0.53 percent with α=0\alpha=0α=0.

  • Interregional trade: a version with traded and nontraded sectors damps real-wage volatility, so matching the employment response requires ϕL=1.72\phi_L=1.72ϕL​=1.72. The output loss rises to 0.73 percent (employment −0.63-0.63−0.63 percent, welfare −0.62-0.62−0.62 percent).

  • Capital and housing: capital is rented at a fixed world real rate and housing is supplied locally as in Suarez Serrato and Zidar (2016). The output loss is 0.64 percent, because flood risk also lowers the capital-labor ratio (by 0.37 percent).

  • Heterogeneous firms: a Melitz (2003) version with fixed operating costs is calibrated to an exit rate of 0.08 and a 0.8 percent flood-induced rise in exits. The output loss is 0.51 percent, slightly smaller, because exiting firms are small.

Across extensions the losses are similar or somewhat larger, so the baseline forces dominate.

Counterfactual 3: Future Flood Risk, 2020-2050

rmr_mrm​ is scaled by First Street Foundation's county projections, under which the share of properties at risk rises by 4.5 percent on average. Output falls by 0.135 percent; employment falls by 0.057 percent, entry by 0.053 percent, exits by 0.037 percent and welfare by 0.055 percent. This is comparable to the 0.11 percent global GDP loss from sea-level rise in Desmet et al. (2021). The decomposition is direct damage 0.013, labor relocation 0.038, labor supply 0.058 and variety 0.026 percent, so only about 10 percent comes from direct damages. The projected risk increase is more positively correlated with regional productivity, so outflows from productive regions amplify the loss.

Takeaways

Expected flood risk, not realized floods, drives long-run firm entry and employment. Most of the output cost of flood risk comes from endogenous labor supply and fewer varieties, and only a minority from direct damages, so damage-based accounting understates the cost of climate hazards. Migration redistributes activity across counties but adds little to the aggregate loss. One caveat is that FEMA zone maps proxy perceived risk, so the paper cannot fully separate perceived from actual risk, or risk from mandatory flood insurance.

This is the long-difference panel regression behind the first stylized fact. It is estimated on two cross-sections only, t∈{1998,2018}t\in\{1998,2018\}t∈{1998,2018}, the two years for which digitized FEMA maps exist. The outcome Yi,tY_{i,t}Yi,t​ is a count or level in locality iii (entrants, exits, employment, population, real GDP), taken in logs, and FloodRiski,t\text{FloodRisk}_{i,t}FloodRiski,t​ is a share between 0 and 1, so β1\beta_1β1​ is a semi-elasticity: moving the flood-zone share by one unit (from no land to all land in a flood zone) changes the outcome by about 100 β1100\,\beta_1100β1​ percent.

With only two periods, the locality fixed effect σi\sigma_iσi​ makes the regression equivalent to a first-difference (change-on-change) regression:

Δlog⁡Yi=β1 ΔFloodRiski+Δγs+ζ ΔXi+β2 ΔActualFloodi+Δϵi\Delta\log Y_{i}=\beta_1\,\Delta\text{FloodRisk}_{i}+\Delta\gamma_{s}+\zeta\,\Delta X_{i}+\beta_2\,\Delta\text{ActualFlood}_{i}+\Delta\epsilon_{i}ΔlogYi​=β1​ΔFloodRiski​+Δγs​+ζΔXi​+β2​ΔActualFloodi​+Δϵi​

so β1\beta_1β1​ is identified from differences across counties of the same state in how much their flood-zone share changed between the 1998 and 2018 maps. The state-by-year effect γs,t\gamma_{s,t}γs,t​ absorbs state-specific trends (and state-level mapping practices), Xi,tX_{i,t}Xi,t​ absorbs differential trends related to labor-market composition and the China shock, and ActualFloodi,t\text{ActualFlood}_{i,t}ActualFloodi,t​ separates the effect of expected risk from the effect of the floods that actually happened, so that β1\beta_1β1​ is not simply picking up accumulated damage.

The identifying assumption is that, conditional on these terms, map revisions are unrelated to other local trends; the placebo on 1990-1998 outcomes, the LASSO-IV and the First Street measure are checks on it. As an illustration, the employment coefficient −0.199-0.199−0.199 times a 0.10 rise in the flood-zone share gives a 2.0 percent fall in employment. The coefficients for employment and population are later the targets of the indirect-inference problem in equation (21).

This is the annual panel regression behind the second stylized fact. Unlike equation (1), the regressor Floodi,t\text{Flood}_{i,t}Floodi,t​ is a realized event, the share of county iii's area that was actually under water in year ttt according to the Dartmouth Flood Observatory, and the panel is annual (2001-2018), so there is within-county year-to-year variation.

The county fixed effect σi\sigma_iσi​ removes everything permanent about a county, including its average flood exposure, that is, its flood risk. What is left in Floodi,t\text{Flood}_{i,t}Floodi,t​ is the deviation of this year's flooding from the county's own norm, compared with other counties in the same state and year through γs,t\gamma_{s,t}γs,t​. Since the timing of a flood, given the long-run risk, is plausibly random, β1\beta_1β1​ is the causal same-year effect of a flood shock. It is again a semi-elasticity: the GDP coefficient −0.005-0.005−0.005 times a one-standard-deviation shock of 0.4 gives a 0.2 percent fall in GDP.

The contrast between equations (1) and (2) is the empirical basis of the model's timing: entry, employment and population do not respond to realized floods (coefficients near zero) but respond strongly to risk, while output responds to both. This is why in the model location, labor supply and entry are chosen before the state sss is known, and floods enter only as ex-post shocks in equation (6). The event estimates are also used directly in the calibration: summing current and one-year-lag effects gives δ=0.006\delta=0.006δ=0.006 from the GDP regression and δk=0.008\delta_k=0.008δk​=0.008 from the exit regression.

The condition follows from the entry decision of a risk-neutral potential entrant in a static (one-period) model. Entry takes place before the state sss is known. It requires hiring fmf_mfm​ units of labor, which are paid the wage of the state that is realized, so the expected entry cost is

∑sPr⁡(s) Wm(s) fm\sum_s\Pr(s)\,W_m(s)\,f_ms∑​Pr(s)Wm​(s)fm​

After the state is realized the entrant is hit by the exit shock of equation (6): with probability κ(s)\kappa(s)κ(s) it exits before producing and earns nothing, and with probability 1−κ(s)1-\kappa(s)1−κ(s) it produces and earns πm(s)\pi_m(s)πm​(s) from equation (7). Its expected operating profit is

∑sPr⁡(s)[κ(s)⋅0+(1−κ(s))πm(s)]=∑sPr⁡(s)(1−κ(s))πm(s)\sum_s\Pr(s)\left[\kappa(s)\cdot 0+\left(1-\kappa(s)\right)\pi_m(s)\right]=\sum_s\Pr(s)\left(1-\kappa(s)\right)\pi_m(s)s∑​Pr(s)[κ(s)⋅0+(1−κ(s))πm​(s)]=s∑​Pr(s)(1−κ(s))πm​(s)

The expected net value of entry is the difference between the two:

Vme=∑sPr⁡(s)(1−κ(s))πm(s)−∑sPr⁡(s) Wm(s) fmV_m^{e}=\sum_s\Pr(s)\left(1-\kappa(s)\right)\pi_m(s)-\sum_s\Pr(s)\,W_m(s)\,f_mVme​=s∑​Pr(s)(1−κ(s))πm​(s)−s∑​Pr(s)Wm​(s)fm​

There is an unbounded pool of potential entrants. If Vme>0V_m^{e}>0Vme​>0 more firms enter, which lowers Pm(s)P_m(s)Pm​(s) and so the profit of each firm; if Vme<0V_m^{e}<0Vme​<0 nobody enters. With positive entry, equilibrium requires Vme=0V_m^{e}=0Vme​=0, which is equation (8).

Two remarks. The condition holds in expectation over states, not state by state, because entry is sunk before floods are realized; this is how flood risk, and not flood events, governs the number of firms. And both sides are weighted by Pr⁡(s)\Pr(s)Pr(s) only, with no marginal-utility weights, which is the risk-neutrality assumption that also makes actuarially fair insurance irrelevant for entry.

This is the realized utility of an individual living in region mmm when state sss occurs. It has three multiplicative layers. vmv_mvm​ is the individual's idiosyncratic taste for region mmm, drawn from the distribution in equation (10). Bm(s)B_m(s)Bm​(s) is the amenity of the region in that state, which falls when there is a flood. The bracket is the consumption-leisure payoff: cm(s)c_m(s)cm​(s) is final-good consumption per unit of labor supplied, so cm(s) lmc_m(s)\,l_mcm​(s)lm​ is total consumption, and the second term is the disutility of supplying lml_mlm​ units of labor, scaled by the regional shifter ψm\psi_mψm​.

The budget constraint is written per unit of labor, Pm(s) cm(s)≤Wm(s)P_m(s)\,c_m(s)\leq W_m(s)Pm​(s)cm​(s)≤Wm​(s). It binds, so cm(s)=Wm(s)/Pm(s)c_m(s)=W_m(s)/P_m(s)cm​(s)=Wm​(s)/Pm​(s) is the real wage, and there is no other income because free entry leaves no aggregate profits (see equation (14)).

The form is of the Greenwood-Hercowitz-Huffman type: utility is linear in consumption net of labor disutility, so there are no income effects on labor supply and no risk aversion over states. With a known real wage www the labor choice would solve

w=ψm lm1/ϕL⟹lm=(wψm)ϕLw=\psi_m\,l_m^{1/\phi_L}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad l_m=\left(\frac{w}{\psi_m}\right)^{\phi_L}w=ψm​lm1/ϕL​​⟹lm​=(ψm​w​)ϕL​

so ϕL\phi_LϕL​ is exactly the (Frisch and uncompensated) elasticity of labor supply to the real wage. Note that lml_mlm​ carries no state index: labor is chosen before the shock, so it responds to the expected real wage, as derived in equation (11). Because amenities multiply the whole bracket, the indirect utility is multiplicative in vmv_mvm​, which is what makes the Frechet assumption deliver the closed-form shares in equation (12) and welfare in equation (13).

The first expression is the distribution of the idiosyncratic location taste vmv_mvm​: a Frechet distribution with unit scale and shape ϕM>0\phi_M>0ϕM​>0, drawn independently across regions and individuals. A larger ϕM\phi_MϕM​ means less dispersed tastes, so people are closer to indifferent between regions and respond more to differences in fundamentals; ϕM\phi_MϕM​ is therefore the migration elasticity. The Frechet family is chosen because the maximum of independent Frechet variables scaled by constants is again Frechet, which gives the logit-like population shares of equation (12) and the closed-form welfare of equation (13).

The second expression is the amenity. These are the two market-clearing conditions that hold in every region and every state.

Goods market. Lm=ΛmlmLˉL_m=\Lambda_m l_m\bar{L}Lm​=Λm​lm​Lˉ is total labor supplied in region mmm and cm(s)c_m(s)cm​(s) is consumption per unit of labor, so Lmcm(s)L_m c_m(s)Lm​cm​(s) is total consumption, which must equal final output Ym(s)Y_m(s)Ym​(s) because the final good is not traded and is used only for consumption (entry costs are paid in labor). that is, all revenue is paid out as wages, to production workers and to the workers who set up firms. Labor market. Labor has two uses. The Nm(s)=Nm(1−κ(s))N_m(s)=N_m(1-\kappa(s))Nm​(s)=Nm​(1−κ(s)) surviving firms each employ lmd(s)l_m^d(s)lmd​(s) production workers, and all NmN_mNm​ entrants, including those that later exit, use fmf_mfm​ units of entry labor. Hence when a flood raises the exit rate, the fixed amount of production labor Lm−NmfmL_m-N_m f_mLm​−Nm​fm​ is spread over fewer firms and employment per surviving firm rises, as equation (15) shows. The wage Wm(s)W_m(s)Wm​(s) is the price that clears this market.

Illustration at the calibrated values (ϕL=1.55\phi_L=1.55ϕL​=1.55, ϕM=0.84\phi_M=0.84ϕM​=0.84, η=0.002\eta=0.002η=0.002, dl^m/drm≈−0.13d\hat{l}_m/dr_m\approx-0.13dl^m​/drm​≈−0.13): the population response is 0.84×(1.645×(−0.1325)−0.002)≈−0.180.84\times(1.645\times(-0.1325)-0.002)\approx-0.180.84×(1.645×(−0.1325)−0.002)≈−0.18 and the employment response is about −0.32-0.32−0.32 per unit of rmr_mrm​. Employment falls more than population because of the intensive margin dl^md\hat{l}_mdl^m​, which is the pattern in the data that identifies ϕL\phi_LϕL​ separately from ϕM\phi_MϕM​ in equation (21).

This is the outer loop of the calibration: an indirect inference estimator for the two elasticities that cannot be read off the data directly. The auxiliary model is the reduced-form regression (1). β^kdata\hat{\beta}^{\text{data}}_{k}β^​kdata​ is its coefficient on flood risk in the actual county data for outcome kkk, namely −0.199-0.199−0.199 for log employment and −0.130-0.130−0.130 for log population. β^kmodel(ϕM,ϕL)\hat{\beta}^{\text{model}}_{k}(\phi_M,\phi_L)β^​kmodel​(ϕM​,ϕL​) is the coefficient obtained by running the same regression on model-generated data: for a candidate pair (ϕM,ϕL)(\phi_M,\phi_L)(ϕM​,ϕL​) the inner loop recovers Aˉm\bar{A}_mAˉm​, Bˉm\bar{B}_mBˉm​, ψm\psi_mψm​ and fmf_mfm​ from 2018 data, the model is re-solved with {rm,1998}\{r_{m,1998}\}{rm,1998​}, and the simulated 1998 and 2018 outcomes are regressed on flood risk.

The objective is the sum of absolute deviations between the two pairs of coefficients. With two parameters and two moments the system is just identified, so the minimum should be close to zero and the choice of norm or weights is immaterial; the reported fit is −0.199-0.199−0.199 against −0.199-0.199−0.199 for employment and −0.117-0.117−0.117 against −0.130-0.130−0.130 for population, so the match is close but not exact.

Identification comes from Proposition 2. By equation (20),

dL^m−dΛ^m=dl^md\hat{L}_m-d\hat{\Lambda}_m=d\hat{l}_mdL^m​−dΛ^m​=dl^m​

so the gap between the employment and population responses is the labor supply response per person, which is governed by ϕL\phi_LϕL​ through equation (19), while the population response given dl^md\hat{l}_mdl^m​ is scaled by ϕM\phi_MϕM​. If ϕL\phi_LϕL​ were zero, employment and population would respond equally. Matching regression coefficients, not the analytical formulas, lets the full general equilibrium, including spillovers to other counties, enter the model moment. The result is ϕL=1.55\phi_L=1.55ϕL​=1.55 and ϕM=0.84\phi_M=0.84ϕM​=0.84; the outcomes not used here (output, entry, exit) serve as tests of fit.
